global.headline: HAMAS AGREES TO DISARM IN 15-POINT GAZA DEAL AS IRAN WAR ESCALATES TO KUWAIT, TRUMP WEIGHS 'MASSIVE' WEEKEND STRIKES
summary: Hamas signed a 15-point Gaza disarmament plan in El-Alamein, Egypt on Thursday — the first time the group has accepted any weapons-surrender framework — brokered by Trump's US-led Board of Peace. Under the roadmap, Israeli and Hamas forces cease military operations immediately while a precise implementation timeline is finalised within 14 days; Israel will withdraw only to the ceasefire-era "Yellow Line" covering roughly 53% of Gaza until Hamas begins handing over weapons, with full demilitarisation projected to take 200-300 days, and governance transferring to the National Committee for the Administration of Gaza backed by an as-yet-undeployed International Stabilization Force. Netanyahu has stayed publicly silent since Trump's announcement, but Israeli officials say the plan falls short of their "complete demilitarisation" demand; UN ambassador Danny Danon warned Hamas must "actually" disarm, since "cosmetic solutions" won't work, and a source close to Netanyahu said he calculates Hamas will ultimately violate the terms and is unlikely to order any withdrawal before October's elections.

The Iran war continued in parallel: Trump convened his Cabinet at Camp David on Friday — his third trip there this term — to weigh how to end the war and bring down petrol prices ahead of November's midterms, with officials saying fresh strikes, possibly "massive" ones, could come as soon as this weekend. Iran's military claimed Friday drone strikes on Kuwait's Ahmad al-Jaber and Ali Al Salem air bases, unconfirmed by CENTCOM or Kuwait, in stated retaliation for a US strike on Qeshm Island that killed members of the Jafari family — a day after a separate Iranian strike killed a worker and severely damaged a Chinese firm's building in northern Kuwait. Trump's approval rating has fallen to a record-low 32% in the latest Quinnipiac poll. Separately, Trump told his Cabinet he blames Minnesota's "grossly incompetent" governor, not Iran, for a coordinated cyberattack on more than 30 water treatment plants — contradicting his own CISA, EPA and FBI investigators, who suspect Iranian involvement; Gov. Tim Walz said Trump "knows exactly who is responsible." Brent crude closed Friday at $87.84/barrel, up roughly 22% for the month; WTI closed at $86.80.
global.geopolitical: Two threads of the same Trump Middle East strategy are diverging in real time — a genuine, if fragile, diplomatic breakthrough on Gaza sits alongside an Iran war edging toward fresh escalation, with Washington unable to convert progress on one front into leverage on the other, and Trump's own instinct to blame a domestic political rival for what his own agencies suspect is an Iranian cyberattack suggesting he is managing the war's optics as much as its substance.
global.socioeconomic: Oil's climb to a 22%-for-the-month gain, driven by the still-unresolved Hormuz standoff and now a fresh Kuwait front, continues feeding directly into Singapore's fuel, transport and imported-inflation exposure, even as a durable Gaza ceasefire — should it survive its 14-day implementation deadline — would remove one, but not the primary, source of the region's war-risk premium.

global.headline: CEUTA MIGRANT CRISIS TOLL RISES TO 57 AS ITALY SUSPENDS SCHENGEN WITH SPAIN
summary: Around 60,000 migrants crossed from Morocco into Spain's North African enclave of Ceuta within a single 24-hour period this week, and the Spanish government confirmed Friday evening that at least 57 have died in the crossing — most by drowning, with others killed in a stampede at the Tarajal breakwater fence. Roughly 48,300 of those who entered had already returned to Morocco by Friday afternoon, but thousands remain despite Ceuta's warning that the territory lacks the resources to feed or house them. Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez travelled to Ceuta on Friday, calling the surge a "violation of Spain's territorial integrity" and pledging to mobilise all available government resources.

Italy's interior ministry, acting on orders from PM Giorgia Meloni and Deputy PMs Antonio Tajani and Matteo Salvini, closed the country's air and sea borders with Spain on Thursday evening, temporarily suspending the Schengen free-movement pact between the two states. Sánchez hit back on X, writing that "solidarity and empathy are optional. Respect for European treaties and the facts is not."
global.geopolitical: A tens-of-thousands-strong border breach followed within 24 hours by one EU member unilaterally suspending Schengen against another marks a new low in European migration-crisis solidarity, testing whether Ceuta becomes a 2015-scale watershed for EU asylum policy or a bilateral Spain-Italy rupture contained to this incident.
global.socioeconomic: A toll of 57 dead in a single crossing event underscores how lethal the Ceuta route remains even as its political fallout — a suspended free-travel pact between two Schengen members — now threatens the passport-free travel architecture that underpins the EU's own internal trade and tourism economy.

global.headline: SRI LANKA SENTENCES TWO EX-SECURITY CHIEFS TO DEATH OVER 2019 EASTER BOMBINGS
summary: A special Sri Lankan court sentenced former police chief Pujith Jayasundara, 66, and former defence ministry secretary Hemasiri Fernando, 76, to death on Friday for criminal dereliction of duty, murder and attempted murder over their failure to act on prior intelligence warnings before the April 2019 Easter Sunday bombings, which killed 279 people including 45 foreigners and were blamed on a homegrown Islamist extremist group. Both men can appeal to the Supreme Court and remain in judicial custody pending bail. Sri Lanka has not carried out an execution since 1976, maintaining an unofficial moratorium even as courts continue to hand the sentence down.
global.geopolitical: The verdict closes, more than seven years on, one of the most consequential accountability questions from an attack that devastated Sri Lanka's tourism-dependent economy and reshaped its security establishment, even though the four-decade execution moratorium means the sentences are unlikely ever to be carried out.
global.socioeconomic: A conviction squarely for institutional failure, rather than for the bombings themselves, reinforces to foreign governments and travellers that Sri Lanka's post-2019 security-sector reforms were a direct response to identified negligence — a framing Colombo has leaned on to help rebuild inbound tourism after the attack's initial collapse.

global.headline: DRC EBOLA OUTBREAK NOW FASTEST-GROWING ON RECORD, SECOND-LARGEST EVER, WHO SAYS
summary: WHO data published Friday show the Democratic Republic of Congo's Bundibugyo-strain Ebola outbreak, first identified in mid-May, has reached 3,553 confirmed cases and 1,558 deaths — surpassing, in just over two months, the total case count of the 2018-2020 DRC outbreak that took nearly two years to reach comparable levels, making it the second-largest Ebola outbreak on record. The Bundibugyo virus complicates the response because existing certified Ebola vaccines and treatments were developed for the more common Zaire ebolavirus species, not this one. WHO officials say most new infections are being traced to unknown chains of transmission, describing the outbreak as "a fire."
global.geopolitical: A record-pace outbreak of a less-treatable Ebola strain, spreading mainly through untraceable transmission chains, tests a global health-response architecture already stretched thin by competing donor and specialist-capacity demands from the Iran war and Europe's wildfire crisis.
global.socioeconomic: The lack of a vaccine or treatment specifically validated for the Bundibugyo strain forces the response to lean more heavily on containment and contact-tracing than the faster, vaccine-driven interventions used in prior Zaire-strain outbreaks, raising both the human toll and the economic cost of containment across the DRC's already-fragile health system.

global.headline: POLAND SUMMONS RUSSIAN AMBASSADOR OVER MISSILE STRIKE AS MOSCOW ESCALATES DELIBERATE ATTACKS ON UKRAINIAN FUEL STATIONS
summary: Poland's foreign ministry summoned Russia's ambassador Friday and handed him a formal protest note after confirming Thursday's 10-metre crater near Tarnawa Kolonia in the Lublin region was caused by a Russian Kh-101 cruise missile that travelled roughly 90km inside Polish territory. A ministry spokesperson said Warsaw conveyed "unequivocal condemnation of hostile actions directed against the security of a sovereign state and its citizens"; Russia has not commented. Separately, a CNN analysis found Russia has struck more than 200 Ukrainian fuel stations since June — averaging roughly three a day — in what Ukrainian officials and residents describe as a deliberate campaign to sow panic and disrupt daily life ahead of winter. Zaporizhzhia alone recorded 54 fuel-station strikes over 24 days to 27 July, killing four people and injuring 29; Ukrainians see the campaign as Moscow's attempt to import onto Ukrainian streets the same fuel queues and shortages that repeated Ukrainian strikes on Russian refineries have inflicted around Moscow.
global.geopolitical: NATO's restrained response to a missile landing 90km inside Polish territory — a formal diplomatic protest rather than any Article 4 or 5 move — again signals the alliance's threshold for direct confrontation has not shifted, even as Russia's parallel fuel-station campaign suggests Moscow is testing how far it can escalate the war's daily-life impact on both sides of the border without triggering that threshold.
global.socioeconomic: A sustained campaign against fuel stations, echoing the queues-and-shortages tactic Ukrainian refinery strikes have inflicted on Russia, threatens to compound Ukraine's already-strained energy security heading into a second wartime winter, forcing civilians into an explicit trade-off between refuelling and personal safety.

singapore.headline: GOVERNMENT TAKES POSSESSION OF LEE KUAN YEW'S 38 OXLEY ROAD HOME, CLOSING A DECADE-LONG FAMILY DISPUTE
summary: The Singapore Land Authority and National Heritage Board said Friday the government has completed compulsory acquisition of 38 Oxley Road, Lee Kuan Yew's former residence, and taken possession of the site — the final step after it was gazetted a national monument on 12 December 2025 and gazetted for acquisition on 29 January 2026. Compensation will be based on the property's market value at the time of the December gazette, though the amount has not been disclosed. NHB will study options for developing the site into a public space, such as a heritage park, "in a manner that respects Mr Lee Kuan Yew's wishes for privacy"; there will be no public access in the interim beyond necessary maintenance works. Lee Kuan Yew's younger son, Lee Hsien Yang, who has long argued his father wanted the house demolished, wrote on Facebook Friday that the "compulsory acquisition of his home is a repudiation of his values and a flagrant disregard for his long-held wish."
singapore.geopolitical: The acquisition closes, at least procedurally, one of the most publicly damaging episodes in the ruling family's history — a decade-long, at-times-litigious rift between PM Lee Hsien Loong and his siblings over their father's estate and legacy — though Lee Hsien Yang's renewed public objection signals the underlying family dispute itself remains unresolved even as the property question is settled.
singapore.socioeconomic: Converting a private residential site in prime District 10 into a public heritage space removes it permanently from Singapore's already-scarce landed-housing stock, a trade-off the government has judged worth making for a monument tied directly to the founding of the state.

singapore.headline: MASSIVE ATTACK MEMBERS BANNED FROM RE-ENTERING SINGAPORE OVER PALESTINIAN FLAG DISPLAY
summary: The Singapore Police Force and Infocomm Media Development Authority said Friday the two Massive Attack members who displayed a Palestinian flag and led "Free Palestine" chants at the band's Wednesday concert at the Star Theatre — understood to be founding members Robert "3D" Del Naja and Grant "Daddy G" Marshall — have received stern warnings and been barred from re-entering Singapore, in an apparent breach of the Foreign National Emblems (Control of Display) Act and the Public Order Act. IMDA said it will not approve any future performance applications from the band and is separately investigating a possible breach of the concert's own licence conditions, with further action to follow once that inquiry concludes.
singapore.geopolitical: A concrete travel ban and licence investigation, rather than the caution issued in similar past cases, signals Singapore hardening its enforcement posture on Israel-Gaza-related expression at ticketed international events, a stance increasingly at odds with the more permissive line Western touring markets have taken toward artists' pro-Palestinian statements.
singapore.socioeconomic: Barring a globally touring act from ever returning, plus a formal licence-compliance investigation into the promoter, raises the compliance stakes for Singapore's concert industry just as it competes with regional rivals to be the default Southeast Asian tour stop for politically outspoken Western artists.

singapore.headline: POLICE OFFICER'S SENTENCE RAISED TO 11½ YEARS OVER FATAL ABUSE OF MYANMAR DOMESTIC WORKER
summary: The High Court on Friday raised suspended police officer Kevin Chelvam's jail term from 10 to 11½ years after allowing the prosecution's appeal against his sentence on one of four charges tied to the 2016 death of Myanmar domestic worker Piang Ngaih Don, who weighed just 24kg when she died after prolonged abuse by Chelvam's then-wife. Chelvam, 46, was convicted of voluntarily causing hurt, abetting his wife's grievous hurt by starving the victim, giving false information to police, and destroying evidence by dismantling a CCTV recorder that had captured 35 days of footage showing Piang beaten, burned with a heated iron, choked and deprived of food and rest.
singapore.geopolitical: A decade-old case that first exposed gaps in domestic-worker protection continues to generate fresh legal developments nearly ten years on, keeping Singapore's foreign-domestic-worker safeguards — a policy area regional labour-sending governments watch closely — under periodic public scrutiny even after the core convictions were settled years ago.
singapore.socioeconomic: The appellate sentence increase against a former police officer, rather than only the primary abuser, reinforces that failing to intervene in or actively concealing abuse carries substantial personal legal exposure — a signal aimed as much at households employing domestic workers as at the justice system's own institutions.

singapore.headline: SHANTI PEREIRA FINISHES EIGHTH IN HISTORIC COMMONWEALTH GAMES 200M FINAL
summary: Shanti Pereira placed eighth in the women's 200m final at the Glasgow Commonwealth Games on Friday, becoming the first Singaporean to reach an individual sprint final at the Games after clocking a season-best 22.81 seconds in Thursday's semi-final. Pereira, the reigning Asian Games 200m champion and Singapore's national record holder in the event, had missed out on a 100m final berth earlier in the Games.
singapore.geopolitical: Reaching, and now completing, a first-ever individual sprint final keeps Singapore's small elite-athletics programme visible on a multinational sporting stage even without a podium finish, the kind of incremental breakthrough smaller sporting nations rely on to sustain athletics funding and public interest between medal years.
singapore.socioeconomic: A historic final berth, regardless of finishing position, feeds directly into the funding and endorsement calculus behind Singapore's Sport Excellence scheme, likely reinforcing the case for continued investment in the country's sprint programme ahead of future Games cycles.

singapore.headline: LAW SOCIETY TO SEEK PRITAM SINGH'S STRIKE-OFF AT AUG 13 DISCIPLINARY HEARING
summary: The Law Society of Singapore confirmed Friday it will ask the Court of Three Judges to strike Workers' Party chief and Aljunied GRC MP Pritam Singh off the rolls as a lawyer when his disciplinary case is heard on 13 August. Singh, a non-practising lawyer, was convicted in February 2025 on two counts of lying under oath to Parliament's Committee of Privileges over former WP MP Raeesah Khan's 2021 falsehood about a sexual-assault case, and lost his High Court appeal in December 2025, paying a $14,000 fine. The bench will comprise Chief Justice Sundaresh Menon, Justice Kannan Ramesh and Justice See Kee Oon; the Law Society is represented by Senior Counsel Cavinder Bull, Singh by Peter Cuthbert Low. Possible sanctions range from censure or a fine of up to S$100,000 to being struck off entirely.
singapore.geopolitical: A strike-off application against a sitting Leader of the Opposition, even one who no longer practises law, keeps a politically sensitive question — whether professional-conduct proceedings against an elected opposition figure risk looking punitive — live in the run-up to a hearing convened by the country's most senior judges.
singapore.socioeconomic: The proceeding carries no direct economic stakes but tests how Singapore's legal profession's self-regulatory bodies handle conduct findings against high-profile political figures, a precedent other professional bodies overseeing MPs in law-adjacent careers may watch closely.

word.definition: The shameful failure to fulfil an obligation or duty; abandonment or neglect of responsibility.
word.etymology: From Latin "derelictio," from "derelinquere" ("to abandon utterly"), from de- ("entirely") + relinquere ("to leave behind, relinquish").
word.example: Sri Lanka's special court convicted the country's former police chief and defence secretary of criminal dereliction of duty for ignoring intelligence warnings ahead of the 2019 Easter bombings — a verdict, delivered more than seven years on, that finally assigns institutional blame for the failures that let the attack happen.
